b: the Lamp Road proper, dwarf paving nine feet wide under a barrel roof, with a lamp station every mile and every station lit two hours before the charts say it should be
c: Keep to the crown of the road.
Drop into the drainage gallery alongside it.
Stop at the fourth station where a courier's barrow is standing.

b: the crown of the road, which runs straight for four miles and can be seen along its whole length by anything standing at either end of it
c: Press on to the cistern dip.
Get down into the drainage gallery out of the sightline.

b: the drainage gallery beside the paving, four feet high and running with spring water, which hides the company and costs it every yard in stooped backs and wet knees
c: Climb out at the cistern dip.

b: the fourth station: a courier's barrow parked neatly, a Warden's shield hung on the lamp bracket with the paint scraped off, and a tally of nine strokes cut into the post with the ninth struck through
c: Cut the tally out of the post for Ilsabet.
Leave it; the barrow is not your business.
Camp here at the station where it is dry and warm.

b: the tally cut free and read: dwarf work, recent, and matching the mark from the Barrow Moor gibbet stroke for stroke, which means one hand keeps both counts
c: Pocket it and go on to the cistern.

b: the cistern dip, where a spring has come through the roof and filled forty feet of the road to chest height, with the lamps on both sides of it still burning under the water line
c: Rope a line and wade it.
Go round by the maintenance crawl and lose an hour.
Have Ilsabet crust the surface hard enough to cross.
Cross dry along the lamp brackets.

b: chest-deep in spring water at a temperature that stops argument, the rope line taut, Ossa holding her lamp-pole above her head with both arms the whole way
c: Keep the line taut and cross one at a time.
Let go and swim the last twenty feet.

b: an hour lost in the maintenance crawl, dry to the knee, and at the crawl's far grating the first sight of the Marchgate two miles on, with all nine of its lamps lit
c: Rejoin the road and make camp.

b: salt and glass and Ilsabet's working voice, and forty feet of cistern crusting over hard enough to bear weight for about two minutes, which is enough if nobody stops
c: Give her a minute, then make camp.

b: the surface stair up over the mountain's shoulder in a whiteout, cut for dwarves and drifted over, with cornices on the left hand and nothing whatever on the right
c: Rope up and take it slowly.
Push the pace and get over before dark.
Follow the beaten sledge trail somebody else cut.

b: the slow way, roped in line with Vurma reading the snow and Ossa's pole probing every step of the drift, six hours to cover two miles and nobody lost
c: Drop off the shoulder at the old workings.

b: the fast way, which works until Weem puts a leg through a snow bridge over a drainage shaft and hangs there on his own rope harness for eleven minutes
c: Slow down; the shoulder made its point.
Keep the pace and let the shoulder try again.

b: a sledge trail beaten flat through the drift, days old, wide as a door, with small hard bootprints on both flanks of it and a smell of lamp oil in the snow
c: Follow it and see what was hauled.
Get off it and back into open snow.
Set an ambush on the trail and wait.

b: the sledge cache at the trail's end: Warden kit sorted by type under a snow tarp, boots in one pile and belts in another, four sledges empty and one still loaded and roped
c: Take the Warden signet and the dispatch tube.
Bury what can be buried and let Nyre say the words.
Back off now; the Skree are still on the shoulder.
Follow the small bootprints back to their camp.

b: a Warden signet and a dispatch tube out of the pile, the tube still sealed, and the seal on it a Reckoning seal rather than a Warden one
c: Get off the trail and go to ground.

b: an hour of digging graves in frozen ground with a moor-iron pick, Nyre's words said properly over nine Wardens, Dellach facing uphill throughout
two hours lying in snow and then nine minutes of violence: five Skree dead in the trail, one of them wearing Warden boots and a bone tally-ring of nine strokes at the throat
c: Take the tally-ring and get off the trail.

b: the old workings under the shoulder, and in a drift-filled adit a body frozen upright: hands bound at the wrist, a strip of iron laid in the open mouth, and snow undisturbed above it for a season
c: Have Ilsabet read the iron in the mouth.
Cover the face and leave the man his iron.

b: Ilsabet reading the strip by lamp: dwarf-cut, a pay-tally, one of nine, and the rank on it the ninth hand, cut with a die she says was struck within the year
c: Make camp while there is light.

b: the old drift, unlit and unmaintained, going down and west under everything, its mouth walled to half height by a survey crew that then took its own wall down again
c: Walk the open drift where the survey pillars stand.
Take the covered gallery where the roof holds.
Back out and rejoin the Lamp Road at the cistern.

b: the open drift with survey pillars every hundred feet, nine notches cut into the third pillar, and a lamp niche beside it holding a clay lamp with oil in it that has not gummed
c: Take the oil; a full reservoir is a full reservoir.
Leave the niche exactly as you found it.
Duck into the covered gallery instead.

b: the lamp decanted, good clean oil, and Vurma saying what everybody has worked out already: somebody services this drift, on a schedule, and will notice a light reservoir before they notice anything else
c: Push on to the camp ground.

b: the covered gallery, dry and echoing badly, its roof holding except at the far end where a fall has closed the way, and something in the rubble of the fall shifting once while you look at it
c: Take the crawl on the left of it.
Back out and take the open drift's lamp niche instead.

b: an hour of moving stone by hand, Dellach and Halt at the face, until the fall gives up a shoulder-width gap that breathes out air smelling of lamp oil and old meat
c: Take the gap while the fall is quiet.
Widen it properly first; do it once, do it right.

b: sixty feet of crawl and then a chamber: nine lamp niches burnt dry, nine hooks, and beneath them a Reckoning courier sitting in a good coat with a chapter seal still at the collar
c: Take the chapter seal off the body.
Back out; nine dead lamps is a message and you have read it.

b: Prior Vask's own chapter seal in your hand, and in the dead courier's satchel nine requisition slips signed by Ferrin Ostwyn, the last of them dated eleven days ago
c: Take it and get out into moving air.

b: the last camp at the eleventh station, two miles short of the Marchgate, with nine lamps burning ahead of you in the dark and the company's mood the specific quiet of people who have stopped asking whether the charts are wrong
c: Cold camp, full watch, no lamps.
Lamps, hot food and a short watch; they need it.
Send Kettle forward to look at the Marchgate.
Break camp and be at the gate before the hour.
Call it. The road has beaten better companies.

b: a cold camp with the lamps out, and at the third hour a courier file goes past on the paving below the station: nine lamps, unhurried, and somebody at the head of it counting in a language with far too many numbers
c: Let it pass and log the hour.
Leave the porters on watch and get an hour's sleep.

b: one lamp, hot food, dry socks and ninety minutes of sleep each in a dwarf station with a working flue, and at the end of it something standing at the edge of the lamplight that does not approach and does not leave
c: Douse the lamp and lie flat until it goes.

b: the challenge given in the Warden form three times, and the shape at the edge of the light answering on the third with a number instead of a name, and then waiting to see whether anybody here knows the next one
c: Say nothing more; hold and let it go.
Answer it. Give it the next number.

b: Kettle back at the second hour with a bad colour: the Marchgate stands unbarred, its nine lamps are trimmed, a Warden's shield is nailed to the gate post as a notice, and the snow inside the arch has boot prints going in and none coming out
c: Walk up to the gate at the hour and go in.
Wait for the next file and go in behind it.
Send her in alone to open the way for the rest.

b: the file comes through at the third hour and the company follows it in at forty paces, moving on the lamp-count off the charts, arriving at the Marchgate with the leaf still swinging

following nine lamps down a dwarf road at forty paces, close enough to hear the count and to hear one member of the file who is not walking under his own management, and the count is not rising, it is going round
c: Keep silent and follow to the gate.
Take the count up with them and walk in as one of nine.

b: the company falling into the file and taking the count, Kettle steady on numbers she learned at eleven, and eleven minutes of that rhythm teaching you the hours, the stations, and what the file is hauling
c: Break off at the gate before the count comes round.

b: camp struck at midnight and the last two miles walked on unlit paving out of the captain's impatience, the company arriving at the Marchgate grey and short-tempered with an hour still to wait
c: Look at what you came for.

b: the Marchgate of Sixteen Mile: a dwarf arch across the whole road with a Warden tower cut into the rock above it, its lintel carved with a door of nine irons, a scraped shield nailed to the post, nine lamps burning, and the gate leaf standing unbarred and open a hand's width exactly as Orr's patrol reported
c: Go in by the open leaf.
Send Kettle up the ventilation shaft and follow.
Have Ilsabet break the mason's postern in the tower.
Sit on the gate and watch it for a full day first.

b: a day spent watching a gate: at the ninth hour two men in Warden cloaks that do not fit them come out, take down three lamps, and carry them back in, and neither of them uses his hands on the leaf
c: Enough watching. Go in by the leaf.
Go up the ventilation shaft where nobody counts.

b: a dry warm camp at the fourth station, and at the third hour the file arrives and stops, and a voice begins a count that includes the sleepers by name in the order they lay down, with the captain ninth

the lamp brackets taken as a dry route across the cistern, and the fourth bracket coming out of nine-hundred-year-old mortar with two of the company hanging from it over water that is deeper than the lamps suggested
the rope let go in spring water cold enough to stop thought, and the cistern's overflow going somewhere the dwarves cut on purpose, and the road going on being exactly as quiet as before

the pace kept and the shoulder's second attempt succeeding: a cornice giving way with three of the company on it, the barrow gone, and Sixteen Mile still two miles off in a whiteout nobody walks out of

the small bootprints followed home to a Skree warren of two hundred under the shoulder, and the company taken alive because alive is what the warren is paid to deliver, and five more marks entered in a tally kept for somebody down the road
the fall widened properly because it should be done once and done right, and forty feet of dwarf gallery deciding, after a century of patience, that this is the hour

the next number given aloud, and the shape at the edge of the lamplight accepting it as an answer and stepping in to complete the transaction, and whatever the Ninth Sword becomes afterwards is counted, kept, and no longer a company

Kettle sent in alone at the second hour and the gate leaf closing to a thumb's width behind her, and after four hours of nothing the company walking back up the Lamp Road without the only person who knew the cadence

an hour's sleep and porters' arithmetic: the watch abandoned, the barrow gone back up the road with the salt and the spare oil, and a company two miles from the Marchgate with nothing left to walk in with

the sensible call made two miles short of the gate, the report written honestly, the fee returned, and nine years of hearing Corrow's chartered company tell the story differently in every station house on the road
the last quarter mile to the Marchgate in the open on dwarf paving, the arch ahead, the Warden's shield on its post catching the lamplight, nine lamps on nine brackets and boot prints going in
c: Walk up the middle of the road in good order.
Come at it along the drainage gallery instead.
Send the barrow up the paving ahead of you and watch.

b: the barrow sent up the paving ahead of the company as an experiment, which rolls to the arch, stops, stands for nine seconds, and then goes in through a gap it cannot fit through, with the salt and the oil still on it
